newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Kim seeks compromise under pressure.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Kim seeks compromise under pressure.

text.p: President Kim Young-sam's about-face over talks with opposition leaders spells the start of compromise over South Korea's controversial labour law to try to limit damage in an election year, analysts said on Monday.
But they said a compromise risked defeating the purpose of the law and turning Kim into a lame duck in the final year of his presidency.
The law aims to free up the labour market and thus cut corporate costs and boost competitiveness.

Kim's softening stance would invite opposition and union pressure to legalise immediately the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, which has led more than three weeks of wildcat strikes, they said.
"President Kim is acknowledging that the ruling camp's hardline gambit was a mistake," Cho Chang-hyun, political science professor at Hanyang University, told Reuters.
"He is now trying to control the damage. He will seek steps to meet some of the opposition demands but he will walk a tightrope not to make himself a lame-duck president," he said.
Kim, due to end his five-year term in February next year, is barred by the constitution from seeking re-election but political analysts expect him to try to install a protege.
Kim agreed to meet opposition leaders on Tuesday to discuss the law, which was rammed through parliament on December 26. He had previously ruled out any compromise.

Opposition parties, seizing on the outcry over the new law, have thrown their weight behind the unionists, calling the wildcat strikes "justified resistance to defend constitutional rights for democracy".
Strikers returned to work on Monday after the confederation said it would limit stoppages to once a week on Wednesday.

"The president appears to be responding to criticisms at home and abroad which he finds difficult to swallow ahead of presidential elections in December," said Kim Young-jin, a fellow at Korea University's Institute of labour affairs.

"He will have to recognise the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions," he said. "Deals also might be struck with opposition leaders for supplementary laws to make it more difficult for companies to lay off workers."
Economists welcomed Kim's readiness for dialogue, but some warned that economic reasoning and not politics should determine any revision of the law.
"Things have been exacerbated by Kim's eagerness to go down in history as a reformer," said Ro Sung-tae, head of the private Hanwha Economic Research Institute.
"But if he makes it difficult for companies to lay off workers and wipe out flexibility of the labour market, the reform would be for the worse, not for the better."

A survey in the monthly magazine Win showed 73 percent of South Koreans opposed the forced passage of the law, which makes it easier for firms to lay off workers and replace strikers as well as bans legalisation of the confederation until 2000.

Many commentators have drawn parallels between President Kim and past military-backed strongmen rulers over the way the bill was railroaded through parliament by the ruling New Korea Party in a dawn session as opposition deputies slept.
Some 53 percent of those surveyed in Win said they would back the opposition in the presidential polls if industrial strife was prolonged.
Pressure on the government has also come from abroad, with the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) joining world trade union leaders in criticising the law.
The Paris-based OECD, which South Korea formally joined in December, has expressed concern over the lack of freedom of association in the new legislation.

Political analysts said hardliners in the ruling party had urged Kim to crack down on strike leaders and paint it as a campaign against worker militancy, something many businessmen cite as a hurdle to boosting production efficiency.
"Traditionally conservative votes are the key in winning presidential elections and the ruling camp might have sought to cement conservative support," said Cho of Hanyang University.
